tasks.title: How to protect your parents from scams: the complete guide
tasks.show: [phone] Your own phone: silence unknown callers, the carrier spam filter, and adding a contact as a favourite.
tasks.narration: Step three, the phone. While you're there, turn on the phone's built-in spam call filtering, and silence unknown callers if your parent is comfortable with that. Set an account PIN with their carrier and turn on number lock or port-out protection if offered. Update the phone's software. And look for remote access apps they didn't install on purpose; if a 'technician' put one there, remove it and change passwords. Fifteen minutes here removes a lot of scam calls before they ever ring.

tasks.title: Identity theft recovery, step by step (what to do in the first week)
tasks.show: [computer] IdentityTheft.gov (typed in): start a report, pick a category, stop before personal details.
tasks.narration: Step three, report it at IdentityTheft dot gov. It's the FTC's official site. You answer questions about what happened, and it creates an FTC Identity Theft Report plus a personalised recovery plan with pre-filled letters. That report matters: it's what you'll show businesses and the credit bureaus to get fraudulent accounts and debts removed. Some creditors may also ask for a police report; your local police can take one, bring your FTC report with you.

tasks.title: Credit freeze vs fraud alert vs monitoring: what you actually need
tasks.show: [computer] Type one bureau's freeze page address and find the freeze button. Stop at sign-in.
tasks.narration: The credit freeze. It stops lenders from pulling your credit report, so most new credit accounts can't be opened in your name. It's free at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion by federal law, it doesn't affect your score, and existing accounts keep working. When you apply for credit, you lift it, online, and the bureaus must do that quickly. The downside is a little hassle when you apply for credit. For prevention, this is the strongest free tool there is.

tasks.narration: Go to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion directly. Make an account at each one and switch the freeze on. Save the logins in a password manager, because you'll need them later.

tasks.title: 2 versions of the toll text scam, decoded
tasks.show: [voice] Read the whole TikTok cut straight through, in your own voice.
lines: Two versions of the toll text scam, and both are after the same thing: your card number.
Version one. 'You have an outstanding toll of three ninety-five. Pay by tomorrow to avoid a fifty dollar late fee.' Then a link. The amount is tiny on purpose, so you pay without thinking.
The link goes to a page that looks like a toll site. You enter your name, address and card. Now they can use that card, or sell it.
Version two shows up weeks later. 'This is your toll agency's fraud team, we saw a suspicious payment.' Now they want your card's security code, or a code texted to you, to 'reverse' it.
Tells in both: a deadline, a fee threat, and a link or callback number you didn't look up yourself. Real agencies bill through your account or by mail.
Don't tap. Type your toll agency's website yourself or use its official app. If you really owe something, it shows up there.
Already entered your card? Call the number on the back of the card, cancel it, and watch your statements. Forward the text to seven seven two six and report it at I C 3 dot gov.

tasks.title: The AI voice clone call: 2 scripts, 1 safe word
tasks.show: [voice] Read the whole TikTok cut straight through, in your own voice.
lines: Two phone calls you'd probably fall for, and the one word that stops both.
Call one. It's your grandson's voice. 'I crashed the car, I'm at the police station, please don't tell Mom.' Then a 'lawyer' takes the phone and asks for bail money.
Voice cloning tools can copy someone from a short clip of them talking online. So the voice really can sound like him. And secrecy, 'don't tell anyone', is the hook that keeps you from checking.
Call two. Your daughter's voice, sobbing, a man in the background saying she's been taken and you have one hour. These 'virtual kidnapping' calls are designed to keep you on the line.
Both fall apart with one question: 'What's our word?' Pick a family safe word tonight. Something not on social media. Say it out loud, don't text it.
No word, or they dodge it? Hang up and call the person back on their real number. In call two, keep them on one phone while someone else calls your daughter from another.
Send this to your parents and grandparents, and set the word together this week.

tasks.title: The fake bank fraud call: 2 scripts decoded
tasks.show: [voice] Read the whole TikTok cut straight through, in your own voice.
lines: Two fake bank calls, and in both the caller ID shows your real bank's number.
They open with something true. Your name, your bank, maybe the last four digits of your card. That's easy to buy after a data breach, so it proves nothing.
Script one: 'We see fraud. To protect your savings, move it to a secure account while we investigate.' They give you an account number. It's theirs.
Script two: 'Someone's sending money from your account. To cancel it, send the same amount to yourself in your payment app.' The 'you' they set up is actually them.
Because you sent it yourself, it often counts as an authorized payment, which makes it much harder to get back.
The fix for both: hang up. Don't call back the number they give you. Call the number on the back of your card, or log in to the app yourself.
If you already sent money, call your bank right away, then report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. Speed matters.

tasks.title: Credit freeze, the full walkthrough (3 bureaus + 2 bonus)
tasks.show: [voice] Read the whole TikTok cut straight through, in your own voice.
lines: Three bureaus, two bonus freezes almost nobody does, and one for your kids. The big three are free by law.
Most identity theft that costs real money is a thief opening a new account in your name. A freeze means the lender can't see your report, so the application dies.
Go to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion directly. Make an account at each one and switch the freeze on. Save the logins in a password manager, because you'll need them later.
Say you apply for a car loan next spring. You log in to the bureau the dealer uses, lift the freeze for a day, and it relocks itself. Online lifts have to happen within an hour.
Bonus round. Innovis is a smaller fourth bureau, and ChexSystems tracks bank accounts. Both will freeze your file if you ask, which helps stop a thief opening a checking account in your name.
Second example: kids. A child's clean credit file is a prize for thieves, and nobody checks it for years. Parents can request a freeze for a child under sixteen at each bureau.
A freeze won't stop someone using a card you already have. For that, turn on transaction alerts with your bank. And check your reports free at AnnualCreditReport dot com.
